data.command: Explain T1547 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution

data.text:
# T1547: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution

**Tactics:** Persistence, Privilege Escalation
**Platforms:** Windows, Linux, macOS

## Overview

T1547 covers adversary techniques for configuring the operating system to automatically execute code when the system boots or when a user logs on. It's one of the oldest and most widely used persistence mechanisms because:

- Autostart locations are **legitimate OS features**, so malicious entries blend in with normal software
- Many autostart entries execute in a **higher-privilege context** than the user who created them (e.g., a Run key under `HKLM` executes for every user, including admins)
- Persistence survives **reboots and logoffs**, giving long-term access

## Sub-techniques

| ID | Name | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| T1547.001 | Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder | `HKLM\...\CurrentVersion\Run`, `RunOnce`, `HKCU` equivalents, and the Startup folder (`shell:startup`) |
| T1547.002 | Authentication Package | DLLs loaded by LSASS at boot via `HKLM\SYSTEM\...\Lsa` |
| T1547.003 | Time Providers | DLLs registered with the Windows Time service (`W32Time`) |
| T1547.004 | Winlogon Helper DLL | `Winlogon\Notify`, `Userinit`, and `Shell` values under the Winlogon key |
| T1547.005 | Security Support Provider | Rogue SSP DLLs loaded into LSASS (can also capture credentials) |
| T1547.006 | Kernel Modules and Extensions | Malicious Linux LKMs (`/lib/modules`) or macOS kexts |
| T1547.007 | Re-opened Applications | Abusing macOS's "reopen windows on login" feature |
| T1547.008 | LSASS Driver | Fake driver registered to load into LSASS |
| T1547.009 | Shortcut Modification | Altering `.lnk` files in autostart paths to point to malware |
| T1547.010 | Port Monitors | DLLs registered with the print spooler (`AddMonitor`) — runs as SYSTEM |
| T1547.012 | Print Processors | Malicious print processor DLLs loaded by the spooler |
| T1547.013 | XDG Autostart Entries | `.desktop` files in `~/.config/autostart/` or `/etc/xdg/autostart/` on Linux |
| T1547.014 | Active Setup | `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components` — executes per-user at logon |
| T1547.015 | Login Items | macOS Login Items, launch agents tied to user sessions |

## How It Works (Common Examples)

**Windows Registry Run key (the classic):**
```
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" /v Updater /d "C:\Users\Public\payload.exe"
```
`HKCU` keys give persistence for one user without admin rights; `HKLM` keys require elevation but persist for all users.

**Startup folder:**
Anything in `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup` (per-user) or `ProgramData\...\Startup` (all users) executes at logon.

**Linux XDG autostart:**
```ini
# ~/.config/autostart/update.desktop
[Desktop Entry]
Type=Application
Name=System Update
Exec=/tmp/.cache/.sysd
```

## Why Attackers Love It

1. **Low friction** — writing a registry value is trivial and often doesn't trip alerts on its own
2. **Privilege escalation path** — a user-level write to an autostart location that executes as SYSTEM (e.g., port monitors, `HKLM` Run keys) escalates privileges at next boot
3. **Evasion** — entries masquerade as legitimate updaters ("Adobe Updater", "OneDrive Sync")
4. **Redundancy** — attackers plant multiple autostart entries so removing one doesn't
